title: Market poems
text:
Pasar Malam

When the sun puts down its heavy bag
and the sky turns the colour of plum,
the street begins to hum.
Lanterns blink awake on poles,
bulbs swing from strings like fat gold beads,
and the smoke from the satay grill
curls up to meet the stars.

A drum of oil is spitting,
a kettle is singing,
a seller shouts, "Hot, hot, hot!"
while a child with sticky fingers
holds a candy-floss cloud
and does not want it to end.

Feet shuffle, coins jingle,
songs spill from a tiny radio.
Everything glows, everything moves,
and the night is wide awake.

Pasar Pagi

Before the roosters clear their throats,
the market is already working.
Trucks sigh in the half-dark.
Crates thump down like heavy footsteps,
and the first mangoes tumble
into piles of orange sunrise.

Aunties bargain in whispers,
weighing tomatoes in careful hands.
A fish lies silver on a block of ice,
still smelling of the sea.
Nobody sings. Nobody dawdles.
There are meals to cook
and breakfasts waiting at home.

Then the sun climbs over the awnings,
and the stalls grow loud and warm.
The sellers stretch, and smile,
and the day has begun.

Pasar Sore

By four o'clock the hurry has gone.
The sellers fold their awnings slowly,
and the last bananas, speckled and sweet,
are sold for half the price.

A boy sweeps peelings into a heap.
A cat sits proudly on a crate
as if the whole place were hers.
The light turns thin and golden,
and the tired voices go quiet.

A mother counts her coins twice,
smiling at the small, round sum.
A child holds a paper cone of peanuts
and shares them with a stranger.
No one is in a hurry now,
and the whole street breathes out.

We carry our bags home, heavy and warm,
and somewhere behind us
the night market is waking up
to begin the whole thing again.
